items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — the call went from 'This is Chris with Einstein loving company. How can I help you?' straight into 'Alright, starting off with special considerations' with no roadmap, no time estimate for the call, and no confirmation the customer was ready. The customer never knew a room-by-room inventory was coming.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up. The first three words after the customer explained his situation were 'Okay. Okay, let me track that down.'
Customer's name never used once. John introduced himself in his first sentence ('hey my name is John') and Chris never said it — not during the call, not at the close. Zero of the 3+ standard.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. 'Insurance' appeared only as a line item inside the inclusions list ('the truck taxes, insurance pans and wraps') with no explanation of the $2,000 repair/replace/reimburse coverage — and this was a call with a glass-top coffee table, two solid-wood dressers, a king bed, a TV, and a media console going down a 150-foot elevator carry.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — a real miss on a Saturday move where the customer is coordinating an apartment move-out and a home move-in on the same day.

Packing services never offered or priced. The customer said 'I don't know we haven't even started packing' and 'Oh, god boxes' — an unmistakable buying signal — and Chris responded by estimating a box count for him instead of quoting the packing service at the same hourly rate plus materials.

'Additional stops' never asked and the storage unit was never resolved. Chris asked 'do you have a garage on site or storage?' and the customer said 'We do have a storage unit that has some boxes in it as well... probably like fifteen in there' plus kitchen glassware boxes — and the call ended without establishing whether that unit is at the apartment complex or a separate address, whether it is a second stop, or whether those boxes are in the 40-box count. That is an unpriced stop sitting inside a $1,550 quote.
Origin and destination addresses/zips never confirmed on the call. Chris worked off 'the Leander area to the south side of town' from the form and never read either address back.

Stairs at the destination never asked. Chris did thorough access work at the apartment (4th floor, two public elevators, truck parking) and then asked nothing about the house he is delivering to — no stairs, no driveway, no walk distance at the drop.
Moving stressors never asked — no version of 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?'
No 'pricing is super simple' opener. The pricing block opened 'Alright. So going over pricing for Saturday the nineteenth the hourly rate is going to be $200...'
Rate framed as a flat crew price, not per-mover-per-hour, and no day-of-week tier explained on a Saturday move — the customer has no way to know what changes if he moves to a weekday.

No full 'no hidden fees' pitch. He covered the deposit angle well ('We don't even hold a credit card to get you on the book... no cancellation fees or rescheduling fees') but never ran the no-credit-card-fee / no-fuel-surcharge / no-assembly-fee list — and the $150 transportation fee makes that pitch more important on this call, not less.

The transportation-fee explanation was incoherent: 'There is going to be a transportation fee at $150 that comes into play once the hourly rate and the move has been completed the hourly rate itself.' The customer said 'Okay' and never repeated it back. He later summarized his own quote as '1.5 K or less' without ever separating the labor from the fee.

No sense-check anywhere in the clock or pricing delivery. Rate, transportation fee, clock start, 2.5-hour minimum, 15-minute increments, typical range, the 7-hour ceiling and the $1,550 number were delivered as one unbroken monologue and the customer's only contribution was a single 'Okay' in the middle of it.

Save Your Ass was customer-initiated, not proactive, and incomplete. It only started because John asked 'Does the price go down if theoretically, like, I was to move like some of the boxes.' Chris then gave a good carload tip but no concrete consolidation examples (loose items in drawers, photos off the walls, kids' toys, garden tools) and no 'does that make sense?' close.

No booking ask. The closest thing was 'So if you wanted to you know get on the books think about it. That's perfectly up to you.' — permission to leave, not an attempt to close. When John said 'let me think about it,' Chris answered 'let us know how you'd like to proceed when we're ready' with no specific follow-up time and no offer to hold the 19th.

Email handoff named but not explained — 'I'll go ahead and get this shout over via email in the next couple of minutes' with no mention of the bolded detail list at the top, and no 'reply with any corrections,' which matters unusually much here because the whole email is a 20-line inventory the customer dictated verbally.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' and no hours or how-to-reach-us on a call that ended undecided.
No Ecobox referral despite 40+ boxes needed, packing not started, and a storage unit already in play.

Estimate padding: Chris stated the typical completion window as 'about three and a half to five and a half hours' and then quoted to 7 ('I would push you closer to seven hours just to set proper expectations... we should be looking at about 1550 or less'). If the job lands at his own 4.5-hour midpoint the customer pays roughly $1,050 against a $1,550 quote — about 32% under, outside the 20% accuracy band, in the conservative direction.
top_strength: The inventory and access discovery on this call was the best part of it and it was genuinely good. Chris ran a disciplined room-by-room sweep — master bedroom, second bedroom, living room, kitchen, dining, patio, garage/storage — and he caught what the customer left out rather than accepting the list as given: 'And just to make sure any coffee tables are side tubs. I didn't hear that come up,' which surfaced a glass-top coffee table, and 'And what style office desk, is it just like table top and legs or anything heavy?' He also refused to accept a bad number off the quote form, which is exactly the behavior that fixes estimate accuracy: 'I just got this for the load up location. It was indicated about a twenty foot walk. Does that include the walk from your current apartment door to the elevator... Our truck is twenty feet seems a little low' — and he worked it to 'probably of a 150 feet give or take,' a 7x correction on a variable that drives real hours. He then pushed further into access nobody had asked about, 'with the elevator can you reserve that for our sole uses or it just publicly to use?', and named the consequence honestly: 'if a lot of people are moving in and now, just that traffic does add an extra time onto the bill.' The budget framing was also strong and brand-right: 'we just wanna set proper pricing expectation. So you can budget for, you know, worst case scenario and there's no surprises on the day of.' The customer's own verdict was 'this was so super helpful to get this like more dial down quote.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Chris did the hard work and then didn't ask for the business. He had built real trust, created legitimate urgency ('Saturdays do book up the quickest and it's just a couple of weeks out'), and removed every risk ('no cancellation fees or rescheduling fees. We don't even hold a credit card') — and then handed the decision back with 'if you wanted to you know get on the books think about it. That's perfectly up to you.' The line he needed, immediately after the no-deposit reveal, was: 'John, since there's no deposit and no cancellation fee, there's no downside to putting your name on Saturday the 19th right now — it holds the crew, and if anything changes you just call me. Want me to lock it in?' He gets one no and loses nothing. Instead a fully-quoted, fully-inventoried job walked off the phone undecided. Second priority: all three differentiators were skipped on a call that was begging for them. The glass-top coffee table and two solid-wood dressers are the No Worries opening — 'That glass top is exactly what our No Worries Damage Coverage is for: up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage, and I'm noting the glass top on your job so the crew brings the right protection.' Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee are 20 seconds each and would have cost him nothing in a 10.7-minute call. Third: the packing signal was left on the table. When a customer says 'we haven't even started packing' two weeks out, the response is 'We can pack for you at the same $200 hourly rate plus materials — most 1300-square-foot apartments run one packing day. Want me to price that alongside the labor-only option so you can compare?' He was literally asked for an itemized quote and never itemized the one service the customer had just admitted he was behind on. Two business risks to fix before this quote goes out: (1) the storage unit is unresolved — roughly 15 boxes plus kitchen glassware, and nobody established whether it is on-site or a separate address, whether it is a second stop, or whether it is inside the 40-box count; that is an unpriced variable in a $1,550 number and a day-of dispute waiting to happen. (2) The 7-hour quote against his own 3.5–5.5 typical range is exactly the conservative-padding pattern we're chasing on estimate accuracy — quote the honest range and use Save Your Ass to move the customer toward the low end, rather than padding to a ceiling. Methodology note on my read: I also flagged the two-mover crew as a judgment question rather than a rubric miss — 14 man-hours across a 4th-floor 150-foot elevator carry with a king bed and 40+ boxes may be a three-mover job, and a third mover would likely cut wall-clock time without much cost difference. That's my inference from the inventory, not something Chris said or got wrong.
phone_presence_notes: Competent, organized and occasionally reassuring — 'No, no, you're good. I got that noted' landed well and the customer ended genuinely pleased — but the warmth was thin: no how-are-you, the customer's name never used once despite him offering it in his first sentence, dozens of bare 'Okay' acknowledgments, and a pricing segment delivered as one long uninterrupted block.
audio_review_reason: The entire pricing and clock segment transcribes as heavily garbled run-on speech ('imp prorated fifteen minute increments', 'so, suck at that first location we're then making. King about a 45 minute drive', 'get this shout over via email', 'they'll hander the reassembly', and a standalone 'Come.'), so pace, clarity and whether the customer actually tracked the $150 transportation-fee condition cannot be judged from text alone.
